a⃗ · b⃗ = |a⃗| |b⃗| cos(θ).title: Dot product from magnitudes and angle
a⃗ · b⃗ = |a⃗| |b⃗| cos(θ).about: The dot product multiplies the lengths of two vectors and the cosine of the angle between them, giving a scalar. It measures how much the two point the same way: zero when perpendicular, |a⃗||b⃗| when parallel, negative when they oppose.
assumptions: θ is the angle between the vectors placed tail to tail, from 0 to π
Neither vector needs a basis: this form is frame free, which is why Mitiguy uses it for work and power
vars: angle between a⃗ and b⃗ when drawn tail to tail, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π

example.problem: A 3 N force acts on a point moving at 4 m/s, at 60° to the force. Find the power F⃗ · v⃗.

a⃗ · b⃗ = b⃗ · a⃗.title: The dot product commutes
a⃗ · b⃗ = b⃗ · a⃗.about: Swapping the two vectors in a dot product does not change it. So the order in a⃗ · b⃗ never matters, unlike the cross product.
assumptions: Holds for any two vectors in any basis, since cos θ is the same either way
related: the cross product does not commute

example.problem: Check a⃗ · b⃗ = b⃗ · a⃗ for a⃗ = x̂ + 2ŷ + 3ẑ and b⃗ = 4x̂ − 5ŷ + 6ẑ.

a⃗ · b⃗ = a_{x}b_{x} + a_{y}b_{y} + a_{z.title: Dot product from components
a⃗ · b⃗ = a_{x}b_{x} + a_{y}b_{y} + a_{z.about: With both vectors on the same orthonormal basis, the dot product is the sum of the products of matching components. It is the quick way to compute one by hand.
assumptions: Both vectors must be written on the same right-handed orthonormal basis; if they are on different frames, convert one with a rotation matrix first
vars: components of a⃗ on x̂, ŷ, ẑ
components of b⃗ on x̂, ŷ, ẑ
related: rotation matrix to put both on one basis

example.problem: Find a⃗ · b⃗ for a⃗ = 2x̂ − ŷ + 3ẑ and b⃗ = 4x̂ − 2ẑ.

|v⃗| = √(v⃗ · v⃗).title: Magnitude of a vector
|v⃗| = √(v⃗ · v⃗).about: A vector dotted with itself is its length squared, since cos 0 = 1. The square root gives its magnitude, such as a speed from a velocity.
assumptions: The basis must be orthonormal for the component sum to equal v⃗ · v⃗

example.problem: A point's velocity is v⃗ = 3n̂_{x} + 4n̂_{y} + 12n̂_{z} m/s. Find its speed.

v^{2} = |v⃗|^{2} = v⃗ · v⃗.title: Speed squared
v^{2} = |v⃗|^{2} = v⃗ · v⃗.about: v^{2} is shorthand for v⃗ · v⃗, the magnitude squared. It shows up whenever no square root is wanted, as in kinetic energy ½ m v^{2}.
assumptions: v here is the magnitude, so v^{2} ≥ 0 always
Taking v⃗ · v⃗ avoids the square root and is simpler to differentiate

example.problem: A 2 kg particle has v⃗ = 2n̂_{x} − 3n̂_{y} + 6n̂_{z} m/s. Find v^{2} and its kinetic energy.

v̂ = v⃗/|v⃗|.title: Unit vector along a vector
v̂ = v⃗/|v⃗|.about: Dividing a vector by its own magnitude leaves a vector of length 1 that points the same way. Unit vectors give directions for axes, projections and line-of-action forces.
assumptions: v⃗ must not be zero: a zero vector has no direction
related: a force of known size along a cable

example.problem: Find the unit vector along v⃗ = 3x̂ + 4ẑ.

θ = acos((a⃗ · b⃗)/(|a⃗| |b⃗|)).title: Angle between two vectors
θ = acos((a⃗ · b⃗)/(|a⃗| |b⃗|)).about: Rearranging the dot product gives the angle between two vectors from their components. acos returns 0 to π, which is exactly the range of that angle.
assumptions: Neither vector may be zero
This gives the angle but not its sense; use the cross product for which way to turn
vars: angle between a⃗ and b⃗ when drawn tail to tail, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π

example.problem: Find the angle between a⃗ = x̂ + ẑ and b⃗ = ŷ + ẑ.

(a⃗ · û) û.title: Projection: the part of a vector along a direction
(a⃗ · û) û.about: a⃗ · û is how much of a⃗ lies along the unit vector û; multiplying by û turns that scalar back into a vector. What is left, a⃗ − (a⃗ · û)û, is perpendicular to û.
assumptions: û must be a unit vector; for any other b⃗ use (a⃗ · b⃗/(b⃗ · b⃗)) b⃗
related: the part of a⃗ perpendicular to û

example.problem: A force F⃗ = 10n̂_{x} + 5n̂_{y} N acts on a block that slides along û = 0.8n̂_{x} + 0.6n̂_{y}. Find the part of F⃗ along the slide.

a⃗ × b⃗ = |a⃗| |b⃗| sin(θ) û.title: Cross product from magnitudes and angle
a⃗ × b⃗ = |a⃗| |b⃗| sin(θ) û.about: The cross product of two vectors is a vector perpendicular to both, of length |a⃗||b⃗| sin θ, the area of the parallelogram they span. Its direction û follows the right-hand rule from a⃗ to b⃗. Moments M⃗ = r⃗ × F⃗ and ω⃗ × r⃗ velocities are cross products.
assumptions: θ is between 0 and π, so sin θ ≥ 0 and û carries the sign
Right-hand rule: curl the fingers from a⃗ toward b⃗, the thumb gives û
Parallel vectors give zero
vars: angle between a⃗ and b⃗ when drawn tail to tail, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π
unit vector ⊥ to a⃗ and b⃗ by the right-hand rule

example.problem: A 50 N force acts at the end of a 0.3 m wrench, at 30° to the wrench. Find the size of the moment about the bolt.

a⃗ × b⃗ = −b⃗ × a⃗.title: The cross product is anticommutative
a⃗ × b⃗ = −b⃗ × a⃗.about: Reversing the order of a cross product flips its direction. So the order must be kept: r⃗ × F⃗ is a moment, F⃗ × r⃗ is its negative.
assumptions: Holds in any basis; the right-hand rule reverses when the order does

example.problem: With a⃗ = x̂ + 2ŷ + 3ẑ and b⃗ = 4x̂ + 5ŷ + 6ẑ, a⃗ × b⃗ = −3x̂ + 6ŷ − 3ẑ. Find b⃗ × a⃗.

a⃗ × b⃗ = (a_{y}b_{z} − a_{z}b_{y}) x̂ +.title: Cross product from components
a⃗ × b⃗ = (a_{y}b_{z} − a_{z}b_{y}) x̂ +.about: Each component of a⃗ × b⃗ uses the other two components of the inputs: x from y and z, y from z and x, z from x and y, in that cyclic order. It is the expanded form of the determinant rule.
assumptions: x̂, ŷ, ẑ must be a right-handed orthonormal basis, and both vectors on it

example.problem: Find a⃗ × b⃗ for a⃗ = x̂ + 2ŷ + 3ẑ and b⃗ = 4x̂ + 5ŷ + 6ẑ.

a⃗ × b⃗ = det[x̂ ŷ ẑ; a_{x} a_{y} a_{z};.title: Cross product as a determinant
a⃗ × b⃗ = det[x̂ ŷ ẑ; a_{x} a_{y} a_{z};.about: Writing the unit vectors in the top row and the two vectors' components below, then expanding the determinant along the top row, gives the cross product. It is the easiest form to remember.
assumptions: Right-handed orthonormal basis
Row order matters: swapping the a⃗ and b⃗ rows flips the sign
related: moment of a force about a point

example.problem: A force F⃗ = 3ŷ − ẑ N acts at r⃗ = 2x̂ + ẑ m from O. Find its moment about O.

x̂ × ŷ = ẑ, ŷ × ẑ = x̂, ẑ × x̂ = ŷ.title: Cross products of the unit vectors
x̂ × ŷ = ẑ, ŷ × ẑ = x̂, ẑ × x̂ = ŷ.about: In a right-handed basis each unit vector crossed with the next, in cyclic order x → y → z → x, gives the third. Going backwards gives the negative, and any unit vector crossed with itself is zero.
assumptions: The basis is right-handed; in a left-handed one every sign flips

example.problem: Find (2x̂ + ŷ) × ẑ.
steps: x̂ × ẑ = −ŷ (backwards in the cycle), ŷ × ẑ = x̂

a⃗ × a⃗ = 0⃗, a⃗ · (a⃗ × b⃗) = 0.title: A cross product with a repeated vector
a⃗ × a⃗ = 0⃗, a⃗ · (a⃗ × b⃗) = 0.about: A vector crossed with itself is zero since sin 0 = 0. And a⃗ × b⃗ is perpendicular to a⃗, so dotting it with a⃗ gives zero. Both are quick checks on a hand calculation.
assumptions: Holds for any vectors; also b⃗ · (a⃗ × b⃗) = 0
related: scalar triple product, zero when two vectors repeat

example.problem: Check a⃗ · (a⃗ × b⃗) = 0 for a⃗ = x̂ + 2ŷ + 3ẑ, b⃗ = 4x̂ + 5ŷ + 6ẑ.

a⃗ × (b⃗ × c⃗) = b⃗ (a⃗ · c⃗) − c⃗ (a⃗ ·.title: Vector triple product (BAC − CAB)
a⃗ × (b⃗ × c⃗) = b⃗ (a⃗ · c⃗) − c⃗ (a⃗ ·.about: A double cross product a⃗ × (b⃗ × c⃗) lies in the plane of b⃗ and c⃗ and can be written with dot products: b(a·c) minus c(a·b). In dynamics it turns the centripetal term ω⃗ × (ω⃗ × r⃗) into ω⃗(ω⃗ · r⃗) − ω^{2} r⃗.
assumptions: The bracketed pair goes first: a⃗ × (b⃗ × c⃗) ≠ (a⃗ × b⃗) × c⃗ in general

example.problem: A body spins at ω⃗ = 2ẑ rad/s about a fixed point O. Find ω⃗ × (ω⃗ × r⃗) for a point at r⃗ = 0.3x̂ + 0.4ẑ m.

(a⃗ × b⃗) × c⃗ = b⃗ (a⃗ · c⃗) − a⃗ (b⃗ ·.title: Vector triple product, first pair crossed
(a⃗ × b⃗) × c⃗ = b⃗ (a⃗ · c⃗) − a⃗ (b⃗ ·.about: With the brackets on the first pair, the result lies in the plane of a⃗ and b⃗. It follows from BAC − CAB with c⃗ moved out front, which flips the sign.
assumptions: Cross products do not associate; mind where the brackets are

example.problem: Find (a⃗ × b⃗) × c⃗ for a⃗ = x̂, b⃗ = ŷ, c⃗ = x̂ + ŷ + ẑ.
steps: Check: a⃗ × b⃗ = ẑ and ẑ × (x̂ + ŷ + ẑ) = ŷ − x̂

a⃗ · b⃗ × c⃗ = a⃗ × b⃗ · c⃗.title: Scalar triple product: swap the dot and the cross
a⃗ · b⃗ × c⃗ = a⃗ × b⃗ · c⃗.about: In a scalar triple product the dot and the cross may trade places as long as the vectors stay in order. The cross is always done first, so no brackets are needed.
assumptions: The result is a scalar; it is zero when the three vectors are coplanar
related: moment of a force about an axis

example.problem: Check the swap for a⃗ = 2x̂, b⃗ = 3ŷ, c⃗ = x̂ + ŷ + 4ẑ.

a⃗ · b⃗ × c⃗ = b⃗ · c⃗ × a⃗ = c⃗ · a⃗ ×.title: Scalar triple product: cyclic order and box volume
a⃗ · b⃗ × c⃗ = b⃗ · c⃗ × a⃗ = c⃗ · a⃗ ×.about: Shifting a⃗, b⃗, c⃗ round in cyclic order leaves the scalar triple product unchanged; it equals the determinant of their components. Its absolute value is the volume of the parallelepiped (box) the three vectors span.
assumptions: Swapping any two vectors (anticyclic order) flips the sign
Zero means the three vectors lie in one plane
related: a⃗ · b⃗ × c⃗ = det[a; b; c]

example.problem: A parallelepiped has edges a⃗ = 2x̂, b⃗ = x̂ + 3ŷ, c⃗ = ŷ + 4ẑ m. Find its volume.

|a⃗ × b⃗|^{2} = |a⃗|^{2} |b⃗|^{2} − (a⃗.title: Lagrange's identity
|a⃗ × b⃗|^{2} = |a⃗|^{2} |b⃗|^{2} − (a⃗.about: The squared size of a cross product follows from magnitudes and the dot product alone, since sin^{2}θ = 1 − cos^{2}θ. It is handy when the cross product itself is not needed.
assumptions: Any two vectors in three dimensions

(a⃗ × b⃗) · (c⃗ × d⃗) = (a⃗ · c⃗)(b⃗ · d.title: Dot product of two cross products (Binet–Cauchy)
(a⃗ × b⃗) · (c⃗ × d⃗) = (a⃗ · c⃗)(b⃗ · d.about: The dot of two cross products expands into four dot products. With c⃗ = a⃗ and d⃗ = b⃗ it becomes Lagrange's identity.
assumptions: Any four vectors in three dimensions
related: the case c⃗ = a⃗, d⃗ = b⃗

example.problem: Find (a⃗ × b⃗) · (c⃗ × d⃗) for a⃗ = x̂, b⃗ = ŷ, c⃗ = x̂ + ŷ, d⃗ = ŷ + ẑ.

a⃗ × (b⃗ + c⃗) = a⃗ × b⃗ + a⃗ × c⃗.title: The cross product distributes over addition
a⃗ × (b⃗ + c⃗) = a⃗ × b⃗ + a⃗ × c⃗.about: Crossing a vector with a sum is the sum of the separate cross products. So the moment of several forces at one point is the moment of their resultant.
assumptions: Keep each product in the same order (a⃗ first)

example.problem: Forces F⃗_{1} = 10x̂ N and F⃗_{2} = 20ẑ N act at r⃗ = 0.5ŷ m. Find their total moment about O.

^{A}dv⃗/dt = v̇_{1} â_{1} + v̇_{2} â_{2}.title: Derivative of a vector in a frame
^{A}dv⃗/dt = v̇_{1} â_{1} + v̇_{2} â_{2}.about: To differentiate a vector in frame A, write it on unit vectors fixed in A and differentiate only the scalar measure numbers, since â_{1}, â_{2}, â_{3} do not change in A. A vector's derivative depends on the frame it is taken in.
assumptions: â_{1}, â_{2}, â_{3} must be fixed in A; if the vector is written on another frame's unit vectors, use the golden rule
vars: reference frame the derivative is taken in
measure numbers of v⃗ on â_{1}, â_{2}, â_{3}
related: golden rule, for vectors on another frame

example.problem: A point's position in N is r⃗ = 3t^{2} n̂_{1} + 4t n̂_{2} + 5 n̂_{3} m, with n̂_{i} fixed in N. Find ^{N}dr⃗/dt at t = 2 s.
steps: Differentiate each measure number: 6t n̂_{1} + 4 n̂_{2} + 0 n̂_{3}

^{A}d(a⃗ · b⃗)/dt = ^{A}da⃗/dt · b⃗ + a⃗.title: Product rule for a dot product
^{A}d(a⃗ · b⃗)/dt = ^{A}da⃗/dt · b⃗ + a⃗.about: The derivative of a dot product is the derivative of each vector dotted with the other. A scalar's derivative does not depend on the frame, but each vector derivative must be taken in the same frame A.
assumptions: Both vector derivatives in the same frame (any frame gives the same scalar answer)
vars: reference frame the derivative is taken in
related: product rule for a cross product

example.problem: In A, a⃗ = t â_{1} + 2 â_{2} and b⃗ = 3 â_{1} + t^{2} â_{2}. Find d(a⃗ · b⃗)/dt at t = 1.

^{A}d(a⃗ × b⃗)/dt = ^{A}da⃗/dt × b⃗ + a⃗.title: Product rule for a cross product
^{A}d(a⃗ × b⃗)/dt = ^{A}da⃗/dt × b⃗ + a⃗.about: The derivative of a cross product is the derivative of each vector crossed with the other, keeping a⃗ on the left and b⃗ on the right. It is how dH⃗/dt = r⃗ × F⃗ follows from H⃗ = r⃗ × m v⃗.
assumptions: Keep the order of each cross product; swapping flips the sign
Both derivatives in the same frame A
vars: reference frame the derivative is taken in
related: product rule for a dot product

example.problem: In A, a⃗ = t â_{1} and b⃗ = t â_{2}. Find ^{A}d(a⃗ × b⃗)/dt at t = 3.

^{A}d(s a⃗)/dt = ṡ a⃗ + s ^{A}da⃗/dt.title: Product rule for a scalar times a vector
^{A}d(s a⃗)/dt = ṡ a⃗ + s ^{A}da⃗/dt.about: A scalar s times a vector a⃗ differentiates like any product: ṡ a⃗ plus s times the vector's derivative in A. The scalar's derivative is the same in every frame.
assumptions: s is a scalar function of time; a⃗'s derivative is taken in A
vars: reference frame the derivative is taken in

example.problem: In A, s = t^{2} and a⃗ = t â_{1} + â_{2}. Find ^{A}d(s a⃗)/dt at t = 1.

^{a}R^{b}_{ij} = â_{i} · b̂_{j}.title: Rotation matrix entries are dot products
^{a}R^{b}_{ij} = â_{i} · b̂_{j}.about: Each entry of the rotation matrix ^{a}R^{b} is the dot product (direction cosine) of one of A's unit vectors with one of B's. Rows go with â, columns with b̂, and multiplying B-components by it gives A-components.
assumptions: Both bases are right-handed and orthonormal
Row i is â_{i}'s components on B; column j is b̂_{j}'s components on A
vars: rotation matrix taking B components to A components

example.problem: B is turned 30° from A about â_{z} = b̂_{z}. Build ^{a}R^{b} and express v⃗ = 2b̂_{x} on A.

^{b}R^{a} = (^{a}R^{b})^{−1} = (^{a}R^{b.title: Inverse of a rotation matrix is its transpose
^{b}R^{a} = (^{a}R^{b})^{−1} = (^{a}R^{b.about: A rotation matrix is orthogonal, so going back the other way only needs a transpose, not a full inverse. Its determinant is +1.
assumptions: Both bases are right-handed and orthonormal
(^{a}R^{b})^{T} ^{a}R^{b} = identity is a useful check on a hand-built matrix

example.problem: B is turned 30° from A about the z axis. Express v⃗ = â_{x} + â_{y} on B.

^{b}R^{a} = (^{a}R^{b})^{−1} = (^{a}R^{b.try: transpose([cos(30 deg), -sin(30 deg), 0; sin(30 deg), cos(30 deg), 0; 0, 0, 1]) [1; 1; 0]

^{a}R^{d} = ^{a}R^{b} ^{b}R^{c} ^{c}R^{d.title: Chaining rotation matrices
^{a}R^{d} = ^{a}R^{b} ^{b}R^{c} ^{c}R^{d.about: To get from D to A through intermediate frames, multiply the rotation matrices in order; the inner superscripts cancel like a chain. This is how a sequence of simple turns (body-fixed angles) builds one orientation.
assumptions: The order matters: matrix products do not commute unless all turns share one axis
related: angular velocities add the same way

example.problem: B is turned 30° from A about z, and C is turned 45° from B about the same z. Find ^{a}R^{c}.
steps: Turns about one axis add: R_{z}(75°)

^{a}R^{d} = ^{a}R^{b} ^{b}R^{c} ^{c}R^{d.try: [cos(30 deg), -sin(30 deg), 0; sin(30 deg), cos(30 deg), 0; 0, 0, 1] [cos(45 deg), -sin(45 deg), 0; sin(45 deg), cos(45 deg), 0; 0, 0, 1]

R_{z} = [cos θ, −sin θ, 0; sin θ, cos θ,.title: Rotation about z
R_{z} = [cos θ, −sin θ, 0; sin θ, cos θ,.about: When B is turned θ from A about their shared z axis, R_{z} takes components on B to components on A. The z components pass through unchanged.
assumptions: θ is positive by the right-hand rule about â_{z} = b̂_{z}
Columns are b̂_{x}, b̂_{y}, b̂_{z} written on A
vars: angle B is turned from A about z
related: b̂_{x} = cos θ â_{x} + sin θ â_{y}

example.problem: A link B is turned 60° about z. A point sits at 2b̂_{x} + b̂_{y} m. Find its coordinates on A.

R_{x} = [1, 0, 0; 0, cos θ, −sin θ; 0, s.title: Rotation about x
R_{x} = [1, 0, 0; 0, cos θ, −sin θ; 0, s.about: When B is turned θ from A about their shared x axis, R_{x} takes B components to A components. The x components pass through unchanged.
assumptions: θ is positive by the right-hand rule about â_{x} = b̂_{x}
vars: angle B is turned from A about x

example.problem: B is turned 30° about x from A. Express v⃗ = 4b̂_{y} on A.
steps: Second column of R_{x}: b̂_{y} = cos θ â_{y} + sin θ â_{z}

R_{y} = [cos θ, 0, sin θ; 0, 1, 0; −sin.title: Rotation about y
R_{y} = [cos θ, 0, sin θ; 0, 1, 0; −sin.about: When B is turned θ from A about their shared y axis, R_{y} takes B components to A components. Note the sign pattern differs from R_{x} and R_{z}: +sin θ sits top right, because the cycle is z → x about y.
assumptions: θ is positive by the right-hand rule about â_{y} = b̂_{y}
vars: angle B is turned from A about y

example.problem: B is turned 30° about y from A. Express v⃗ = 2b̂_{z} on A.
steps: Third column of R_{y}: b̂_{z} = sin θ â_{x} + cos θ â_{z}

b̂_{x} = cos θ â_{x} + sin θ â_{y}.title: B's x unit vector on A, turned about z
b̂_{x} = cos θ â_{x} + sin θ â_{y}.about: When B is turned θ about z, b̂_{x} has cos θ along â_{x} (adjacent) and sin θ along â_{y} (opposite), straight from SohCahToa. It is the first column of R_{z}.
assumptions: θ measured from â_{x} toward â_{y} (right-hand rule about z)
related: b̂_{y} = −sin θ â_{x} + cos θ â_{y}

example.problem: A 2 m arm along b̂_{x} is turned 40° from â_{x}. Find its tip on A.

b̂_{y} = −sin θ â_{x} + cos θ â_{y}.title: B's y unit vector on A, turned about z
b̂_{y} = −sin θ â_{x} + cos θ â_{y}.about: b̂_{y} is b̂_{x} turned a further 90°, so it leans back toward −â_{x} by sin θ. It is the second column of R_{z}.
assumptions: θ measured from â_{x} toward â_{y} (right-hand rule about z)
vars: angle B is turned from A about z
related: b̂_{x} = cos θ â_{x} + sin θ â_{y}

example.problem: B is turned 40° about z. Express v⃗ = 3b̂_{y} on A.

^{A}dv⃗/dt = ^{B}dv⃗/dt + ^{A}ω⃗^{B} × v.title: Golden rule: derivatives in two frames
^{A}dv⃗/dt = ^{B}dv⃗/dt + ^{A}ω⃗^{B} × v.about: A vector's derivative in A is its derivative in B plus B's angular velocity in A crossed with it. Use it when the vector is easy to write on B's unit vectors but the derivative is wanted in A, such as an inertial frame.
assumptions: Holds for any vector and any two frames
If v⃗ is fixed in B, ^{B}dv⃗/dt = 0 and only ω⃗ × v⃗ is left
vars: angular velocity of B in A

example.problem: B spins in A at ^{A}ω⃗^{B} = 2b̂_{z} rad/s. A rod fixed in B is r⃗ = 3b̂_{x} m. Find ^{A}dr⃗/dt.
steps: ^{B}dr⃗/dt = 0 since r⃗ is fixed in B

^{A}ω⃗^{B} = ±θ̇ λ̂.title: Simple angular velocity
^{A}ω⃗^{B} = ±θ̇ λ̂.about: When B turns relative to A about one axis λ̂ fixed in both, its angular velocity is the turn rate θ̇ along that axis. The sign is + when θ grows by the right-hand rule about λ̂.
assumptions: λ̂ stays fixed in both A and B (a hinge or a single-axis turn)
θ̇ in rad/s
vars: angular velocity of B in A
unit vector along the shared axis

example.problem: A wheel spins on a fixed axle n̂_{z} at 120 rpm. Find ^{N}ω⃗^{W}.

^{A}ω⃗^{D} = ^{A}ω⃗^{B} + ^{B}ω⃗^{C} + ^.title: Angular velocity addition theorem
^{A}ω⃗^{D} = ^{A}ω⃗^{B} + ^{B}ω⃗^{C} + ^.about: Angular velocities through a chain of frames add as vectors, each relative to the frame before it. It builds the angular velocity of a gimbal, robot arm or spinning top from simple single-axis spins.
assumptions: Each term is relative to the previous frame in the chain
Angular accelerations do NOT simply add this way
vars: angular velocity of B in A

example.problem: A gimbal has ^{A}ω⃗^{B} = 2ẑ, ^{B}ω⃗^{C} = 3ŷ and ^{C}ω⃗^{D} = 1x̂ rad/s (on the instantaneous axes). Find |^{A}ω⃗^{D}|.

^{A}ω⃗^{B} = −^{B}ω⃗^{A}.title: Angular velocity reversed
^{A}ω⃗^{B} = −^{B}ω⃗^{A}.about: B's angular velocity in A is the negative of A's angular velocity in B. Seen from the wheel, the car turns the other way.
assumptions: Any two frames
vars: angular velocity of B in A
angular velocity of A in B

example.problem: A wheel W spins in the car C at ^{C}ω⃗^{W} = 10ŷ rad/s. Find ^{W}ω⃗^{C}.

^{A}α⃗^{B} = ^{A}d(^{A}ω⃗^{B})/dt = ^{B}.title: Angular acceleration, in either frame
^{A}α⃗^{B} = ^{A}d(^{A}ω⃗^{B})/dt = ^{B}.about: B's angular acceleration in A is the derivative of ^{A}ω⃗^{B} in A. By the golden rule the derivative in B is the same, since ω⃗ × ω⃗ = 0, so pick whichever frame makes ω⃗ easiest to differentiate.
assumptions: Only A and B are interchangeable here; a third frame adds a cross-product term
vars: angular acceleration of B in A
angular velocity of B in A

example.problem: B spins in A with ^{A}ω⃗^{B} = 3t^{2} b̂_{z} rad/s. Find ^{A}α⃗^{B} at t = 2 s.
steps: Differentiate in B: b̂_{z} is fixed in B, so α⃗ = 6t b̂_{z}

^{P}r⃗^{Q} = −^{Q}r⃗^{P}.title: Reversing a position vector
^{P}r⃗^{Q} = −^{Q}r⃗^{P}.about: ^{P}r⃗^{Q} points from P to Q; reversing the points reverses the vector. Mitiguy writes the start point on the left superscript and the end on the right.
assumptions: P and Q are points; no frame is needed for a position vector
vars: position vector from P to Q

^{Q_{1}}r⃗^{Q_{4}} = ^{Q_{3}}r⃗^{Q_{4}}.title: Adding position vectors
^{Q_{1}}r⃗^{Q_{4}} = ^{Q_{3}}r⃗^{Q_{4}}.about: To get from Q_{1} to Q_{4}, chain the steps through the points in between and add the vectors. Inner points match up like dominoes, which is a quick check on the order.
assumptions: Points only; position vectors need no frame, though each step may be easiest on a different basis
vars: position vector from Q_{i} to Q_{j}

example.problem: A robot arm goes 1 m along x̂ from the base Q_{1} to Q_{2}, 2 m along ŷ to Q_{3} and 3 m along ẑ to the tool Q_{4}. Find ^{Q_{1}}r⃗^{Q_{4}}.

d = |^{P}r⃗^{Q}| = √(^{P}r⃗^{Q} · ^{P}r⃗.title: Distance between two points
d = |^{P}r⃗^{Q}| = √(^{P}r⃗^{Q} · ^{P}r⃗.about: The distance from P to Q is the magnitude of the position vector between them, the square root of the vector dotted with itself.
assumptions: The basis must be orthonormal for the component sum of squares
vars: position vector from P to Q

example.problem: ^{P}r⃗^{Q} = 2x̂ − 3ŷ + 6ẑ m. How far apart are P and Q?

^{N}v⃗^{Q} = ^{N}d(^{N_{o}}r⃗^{Q})/dt.title: Velocity: derivative of position in N
^{N}v⃗^{Q} = ^{N}d(^{N_{o}}r⃗^{Q})/dt.about: Q's velocity in frame N is the derivative, in N, of its position from a point N_{o} fixed in N. Velocity always names a frame because a vector's derivative depends on it.
assumptions: N_{o} must be fixed in N (any such point gives the same answer)
The derivative is taken in N; use the golden rule if r⃗ is on another frame's unit vectors
related: v⃗ = ṙ r̂ + r θ̇ θ̂

example.problem: A point moves in N with ^{N_{o}}r⃗^{Q} = 2t^{2} n̂_{x} + 3t n̂_{y} m. Find its velocity and speed at t = 2 s.

^{N}a⃗^{Q} = ^{N}d(^{N}v⃗^{Q})/dt.title: Acceleration: derivative of velocity in N
^{N}a⃗^{Q} = ^{N}d(^{N}v⃗^{Q})/dt.about: Q's acceleration in N is the derivative in N of its velocity in N. Both derivatives must be in the same frame; Newton's law F⃗ = m ^{N}a⃗ needs N to be inertial.
assumptions: Both derivatives in the same frame N

example.problem: A ball's velocity in N is ^{N}v⃗^{Q} = 10n̂_{x} + (20 − 9.8t) n̂_{y} m/s. Find its acceleration.
steps: Differentiate each measure number: 0 n̂_{x} − 9.8 n̂_{y}

^{N}v⃗^{Q} = ^{N}v⃗^{B_{o}} + ^{N}ω⃗^{B}.title: Velocity of two points on one rigid body
^{N}v⃗^{Q} = ^{N}v⃗^{B_{o}} + ^{N}ω⃗^{B}.about: For two points fixed on the same rigid body, the velocity of one is the other's velocity plus ω⃗ × r⃗ between them. It finds any point's velocity on a link, wheel or gear from one known point.
assumptions: B_{o} and Q are both fixed on rigid body B
If Q moves on B, add ^{B}v⃗^{Q}
vars: angular velocity of body B in N

example.problem: A wheel of radius 0.4 m rolls without slipping: its centre B_{o} moves at 2n̂_{x} m/s and ^{N}ω⃗^{B} = −5n̂_{z} rad/s. Find the velocity of the top point Q, at 0.4n̂_{y} m from B_{o}.

^{N}a⃗^{Q} = ^{N}a⃗^{B_{o}} + ^{N}α⃗^{B}.title: Acceleration of two points on one rigid body
^{N}a⃗^{Q} = ^{N}a⃗^{B_{o}} + ^{N}α⃗^{B}.about: For two points fixed on one rigid body, the acceleration of Q is B_{o}'s plus a tangential term α⃗ × r⃗ and a centripetal term ω⃗ × (ω⃗ × r⃗) pointing back toward B_{o}.
assumptions: B_{o} and Q are both fixed on rigid body B
If Q moves on B, use the one-point-moving form with the Coriolis term
vars: angular acceleration of B in N
angular velocity of body B in N

example.problem: A bar pinned at B_{o} turns with ω⃗ = 4n̂_{z} rad/s and α⃗ = 3n̂_{z} rad/s^{2}. Find the acceleration of its tip Q at 0.5b̂_{x} m (with b̂_{x} = n̂_{x} at this instant).

^{N}v⃗^{Q} = ^{N}v⃗^{B_{o}} + ^{N}ω⃗^{B}.title: Velocity of a point moving on a body
^{N}v⃗^{Q} = ^{N}v⃗^{B_{o}} + ^{N}ω⃗^{B}.about: When Q slides along a moving body B, its velocity in N is the velocity of the body point it is passing over, plus Q's own velocity relative to B.
assumptions: B_{o} is fixed on B; Q moves relative to B
^{B}v⃗^{Q} is Q's velocity as seen by an observer riding on B
vars: angular velocity of body B in N
velocity of Q relative to B

example.problem: A rod B turns about a fixed pin B_{o} at ω⃗ = 2n̂_{z} rad/s. A bead Q is 0.3 m out along it and sliding outward at 0.5 m/s. Find ^{N}v⃗^{Q} (rod along n̂_{x} at this instant).

^{N}a⃗^{Q} = ^{N}a⃗^{B_{o}} + ^{N}α⃗^{B}.title: Acceleration of a point moving on a body (Coriolis)
^{N}a⃗^{Q} = ^{N}a⃗^{B_{o}} + ^{N}α⃗^{B}.about: For Q moving on a moving body B, the acceleration in N has five parts: B_{o}'s acceleration, tangential α⃗ × r⃗, centripetal ω⃗ × (ω⃗ × r⃗), the Coriolis term 2ω⃗ × ^{B}v⃗^{Q}, and Q's acceleration relative to B.
assumptions: r⃗ = ^{B_{o}}r⃗^{Q} with B_{o} fixed on B
The Coriolis term vanishes only if Q is still on B or moves parallel to ω⃗
vars: angular acceleration of B in N
angular velocity of body B in N
velocity of Q relative to B
acceleration of Q relative to B

example.problem: The rod turns steadily at ω⃗ = 2n̂_{z} rad/s about fixed B_{o}; the bead is 0.3 m out, sliding outward at a steady 0.5 m/s (rod along n̂_{x} now). Find ^{N}a⃗^{Q}.

v⃗ = ṙ r̂ + r θ̇ θ̂.title: Velocity in polar coordinates
v⃗ = ṙ r̂ + r θ̇ θ̂.about: In polar coordinates the velocity has a radial part ṙ, from the distance changing, and a transverse part r θ̇, from the line turning. It follows from the golden rule with r̂ turning at θ̇.
assumptions: Planar motion about a fixed origin
θ̇ in rad/s
vars: unit vector ⊥ r̂, toward increasing θ

example.problem: A slider on a turning arm is at r = 2 m, moving out at ṙ = 0.5 m/s, while the arm turns at θ̇ = 3 rad/s. Find its speed.

a⃗ = (r̈ − r θ̇^{2}) r̂ + (r θ̈ + 2 ṙ θ̇.title: Acceleration in polar coordinates
a⃗ = (r̈ − r θ̇^{2}) r̂ + (r θ̈ + 2 ṙ θ̇.about: The radial part is r̈ less the centripetal r θ̇^{2}; the transverse part is r θ̈ plus the Coriolis 2 ṙ θ̇. Use it for anything on a turning arm or in orbit.
assumptions: Planar motion about a fixed origin
Angles in radians
vars: unit vector ⊥ r̂, toward increasing θ
related: v⃗ = ṙ r̂ + r θ̇ θ̂

example.problem: The slider is at r = 2 m with ṙ = 0.5 m/s, r̈ = 0, and the arm turns steadily at θ̇ = 3 rad/s (θ̈ = 0). Find a⃗.

a⃗ = v̇ t̂ + (v^{2}/ρ) n̂.title: Acceleration along a path (tangential and normal)
a⃗ = v̇ t̂ + (v^{2}/ρ) n̂.about: Along a curved path the acceleration splits into v̇ along the path, which changes the speed, and v^{2}/ρ toward the centre of curvature, which turns the velocity.
assumptions: t̂ is along the velocity, n̂ points to the centre of curvature
ρ is the radius of curvature at that point

example.problem: A car on a 50 m radius curve is at 20 m/s and braking at 3 m/s^{2}. Find its acceleration and its size.

^{F}v⃗^{B_{A}} = ^{F}v⃗^{A_{B}}.title: Rolling without slip: the contact points move together
^{F}v⃗^{B_{A}} = ^{F}v⃗^{A_{B}}.about: When body B rolls on body A without slipping, B's point touching A and A's point touching B have the same velocity in any frame F. On fixed ground the wheel's contact point is momentarily at rest.
assumptions: No slip at the contact; sliding allows tangential velocities to differ
B_{A} is the point of B touching A; A_{B} the point of A touching B
vars: velocity of B's contact point in F
velocity of A's contact point in F
related: the centre of a rolling wheel
find the rest of the wheel

example.problem: A 0.3 m radius wheel rolls on fixed ground with its centre at 6 m/s. Find its spin rate.

^{F}ω^{A} r_{A} = ± ^{F}ω^{B} r_{B}.title: Gear ratio from pitch radii
^{F}ω^{A} r_{A} = ± ^{F}ω^{B} r_{B}.about: Meshing gears share the speed of their contact point, so ω × r is equal for both. External gears turn opposite ways (−), a gear inside a ring gear the same way (+).
assumptions: No slip at the pitch point
Both rates measured in the same frame F, usually the housing
vars: angular speed of gear A in F
angular speed of gear B in F

example.problem: A 40 mm pinion turns at 300 rpm and drives a 120 mm external gear. Find the gear's speed.

a = α r.title: Rolling wheel: centre acceleration
a = α r.about: A wheel rolling without slip on a straight, fixed surface has its centre accelerating at α r, from differentiating v = ω r.
assumptions: No slip on a fixed, straight surface
α in rad/s^{2}

example.problem: A 0.35 m radius wheel speeds up its spin at α = 4 rad/s^{2} while rolling. Find its centre's acceleration.

m^{S} = Σ_{i=1}^{n} m^{Q_{i}}.title: Total mass of a system
m^{S} = Σ_{i=1}^{n} m^{Q_{i}}.about: A system's mass is the sum of the masses of its particles or bodies.
assumptions: Mass is constant (no mass entering or leaving)

example.problem: A system has particles of 2 kg, 3 kg and 5 kg. Find its mass.

^{O}r⃗^{S_{cm}} = (1/m^{S}) Σ_{i=1}^{n}.title: Mass centre of a system
^{O}r⃗^{S_{cm}} = (1/m^{S}) Σ_{i=1}^{n}.about: The mass centre is the mass-weighted average of the particles' positions from any point O. For a continuous body the sum becomes an integral.
assumptions: O may be any point; the mass centre found is the same
vars: position of the mass centre from O

example.problem: Particles of 2 kg at (0, 0), 3 kg at (1, 0) and 5 kg at (0, 2) m. Find the mass centre.

m^{S} ^{N}v⃗^{S_{cm}} = Σ_{i=1}^{n} m^{Q.title: Linear momentum and the mass centre's velocity
m^{S} ^{N}v⃗^{S_{cm}} = Σ_{i=1}^{n} m^{Q.about: The system's total linear momentum equals its mass times the mass centre's velocity. So the mass centre moves as if all the mass were there.
assumptions: Constant masses; all velocities in the same frame N
vars: velocity of the mass centre in N

example.problem: A 2 kg cart moves at 3 m/s and a 3 kg cart at −1 m/s along one track. Find the mass centre's velocity.

m^{S} ^{N}a⃗^{S_{cm}} = Σ_{i=1}^{n} m^{Q.title: Mass centre's acceleration
m^{S} ^{N}a⃗^{S_{cm}} = Σ_{i=1}^{n} m^{Q.about: The mass-weighted sum of the particles' accelerations is the total mass times the mass centre's acceleration. With Newton's law this gives ΣF⃗_{ext} = m^{S} ^{N}a⃗^{S_{cm}}.
assumptions: Constant masses; N inertial when used with forces
vars: acceleration of the mass centre in N

example.problem: A 2 kg particle falls at −9.8ŷ m/s^{2} while a 3 kg particle accelerates at 4x̂ m/s^{2}. Find the mass centre's acceleration.

I⃡^{Q∕O} = m^{Q} [1⃡ (^{O}r⃗^{Q} · ^{O}r.title: Inertia dyadic of a particle
I⃡^{Q∕O} = m^{Q} [1⃡ (^{O}r⃗^{Q} · ^{O}r.about: A particle's inertia dyadic about O is its mass times (r^{2} 1⃡ − r⃗ r⃗). Its diagonal entries are moments of inertia and its off-diagonal entries products of inertia.
assumptions: 1⃡ is the unit dyadic (identity); r⃗ r⃗ is the outer product of the position with itself
Mitiguy's products include the minus sign: I_{xy} = −m x y
vars: inertia dyadic of Q about O

example.problem: A 2 kg particle sits at r⃗ = x̂ + 2ŷ m from O. Find its inertia matrix about O.

I⃡^{S∕O} = Σ_{i=1}^{n} I⃡^{Q_{i}∕O}.title: Inertia of a system: add the parts
I⃡^{S∕O} = Σ_{i=1}^{n} I⃡^{Q_{i}∕O}.about: The inertia dyadic of a system about a point is the sum of its parts' dyadics about that same point. Shift each part to the common point first.
assumptions: Every term must be about the same point O and on the same basis
vars: inertia dyadic of system S about O
inertia dyadic of part Q_{i} about O
related: shift a part to O first

example.problem: 1 kg particles sit at x̂ m and ŷ m from O. Find the system's moments of inertia about O.
steps: Products are zero (each has a zero coordinate)
example.answer: I_{xx} = I_{yy} = 1 kg·m^{2}, I_{zz} = 2 kg·m^{2}, products 0

I_{ûû}^{S∕O} = û · I⃡^{S∕O} · û.title: Moment of inertia about any axis
I_{ûû}^{S∕O} = û · I⃡^{S∕O} · û.about: Dotting the inertia dyadic with a unit vector on both sides gives the moment of inertia about the line through O along û. One dyadic thus holds the moment about every axis through O.
assumptions: û must be a unit vector
The axis passes through O
vars: moment of inertia about the û axis through O
unit vector giving the axis direction

example.problem: [I] = [4, −1, 0; −1, 2, 0; 0, 0, 5] kg·m^{2} about O. Find the moment about û = (x̂ + ŷ)/√2.

I_{ûv̂}^{S∕O} = û · I⃡^{S∕O} · v̂.title: Product of inertia for two directions
I_{ûv̂}^{S∕O} = û · I⃡^{S∕O} · v̂.about: Dotting the dyadic with two different, perpendicular unit vectors gives the product of inertia for that pair. A zero product for every pair means the axes are principal.
assumptions: û and v̂ are perpendicular unit vectors
vars: product of inertia for û, v̂ about O
unit vector giving the axis direction

I_{ûû}^{S∕O} = Σ_{i=1}^{n} m^{Q_{i}} d_{.title: Moment of inertia from distances to the axis
I_{ûû}^{S∕O} = Σ_{i=1}^{n} m^{Q_{i}} d_{.about: The moment of inertia about an axis is each mass times its squared perpendicular distance from the axis, summed. d_{i} = |r⃗ × û| is that distance.
assumptions: d_{i} is the perpendicular distance to the axis, not the distance to O
vars: moment about the û axis through O
distance of Q_{i} from the axis

example.problem: A 2 kg mass is 1 m and a 3 kg mass is 2 m from a shaft. Find the moment of inertia about the shaft.

I_{ûv̂}^{S∕O} = −Σ_{i=1}^{n} m^{Q_{i}} δ.title: Product of inertia from coordinates
I_{ûv̂}^{S∕O} = −Σ_{i=1}^{n} m^{Q_{i}} δ.about: The product of inertia is minus the sum of each mass times its two coordinates along û and v̂. It is zero when the mass is balanced about the û–v̂ axes.
assumptions: û ⊥ v̂
Mitiguy's sign: the minus sign is built into the product
vars: coordinates of Q_{i} along û and v̂

example.problem: Masses of 2 kg at (1, 2) m and 3 kg at (−1, 1) m. Find I_{xy} about O.

I⃡^{S∕P} = I⃡^{S∕S_{cm}} + m^{S} [1⃡ (^{.title: Parallel axis theorem for the inertia dyadic
I⃡^{S∕P} = I⃡^{S∕S_{cm}} + m^{S} [1⃡ (^{.about: The inertia dyadic about any point P is the one about the mass centre plus that of a particle of the whole mass placed at the mass centre. It shifts every moment and product at once.
assumptions: One of the two points must be the mass centre; to go between two other points, go through S_{cm}
vars: inertia dyadic about the mass centre
position of the mass centre from P

example.problem: A 4 kg body has [I^{S∕S_{cm}}] = identity (1 kg·m^{2} each, no products). Its mass centre is at x̂ + ŷ m from P. Find [I^{S∕P}].

I_{ûû}^{S∕O} = I_{ûû}^{S∕S_{cm}} + m^{S}.title: Parallel axis theorem for one moment
I_{ûû}^{S∕O} = I_{ûû}^{S∕S_{cm}} + m^{S}.about: The moment about any axis is the moment about the parallel axis through the mass centre plus m d^{2}. The mass-centre axis always gives the smallest moment of its family.
assumptions: The two axes are parallel and one passes through the mass centre
d is the perpendicular distance between them
vars: moment about the axis through O
moment about the parallel axis through the mass centre

example.problem: A 2 kg rod 1 m long. Find its moment about a perpendicular axis through one end.

I_{xy}^{S∕O} = I_{xy}^{S∕S_{cm}} − m^{S}.title: Parallel axis theorem for a product
I_{xy}^{S∕O} = I_{xy}^{S∕S_{cm}} − m^{S}.about: Shifting a product of inertia adds minus the mass times the mass centre's two coordinates from O. Unlike a moment, the shift can be negative, so a product can grow or shrink.
assumptions: x_{cm}, y_{cm} are the mass centre's coordinates measured from O
Mitiguy's sign: I_{xy} = −Σ m x y

example.problem: A 3 kg symmetric plate (I_{xy} = 0 about its centre) has its mass centre at (0.2, 0.1) m from O. Find I_{xy} about O.

[I] = [I_{xx}, I_{xy}, I_{xz}; I_{xy}, I.title: Inertia matrix
[I] = [I_{xx}, I_{xy}, I_{xz}; I_{xy}, I.about: Writing the dyadic on three unit vectors gives a symmetric 3 × 3 matrix: moments on the diagonal, products off it. It depends on the point and the axes chosen.
assumptions: Symmetric: I_{xy} = I_{yx} and so on
Mitiguy's products carry the minus sign, so the matrix is entered as is
vars: moments of inertia about the axes

example.problem: A 1 kg particle is at (1, 1, 0) m from O. Write [I] about O.

I_{xx} = Σ m (y^{2} + z^{2}).title: Moment of inertia about x
I_{xx} = Σ m (y^{2} + z^{2}).about: The moment about the x axis uses each mass's squared distance from that axis, y^{2} + z^{2}. The x coordinate plays no part.
assumptions: Coordinates measured from the point the axis goes through

example.problem: Masses of 2 kg at (1, 2, 2) m and 1 kg at (0, 1, 0) m. Find I_{xx}.

I_{xy} = −Σ m x y.title: Product of inertia, Mitiguy's sign
I_{xy} = −Σ m x y.about: Mitiguy defines the product of inertia with a minus sign, so it can be entered straight into the inertia matrix. Some books drop the sign and put it in the matrix instead; check which a source uses.
assumptions: Coordinates from the point the axes go through
Zero when the body is symmetric about the x–z or y–z plane

example.problem: Masses of 2 kg at (1, 2, 2) m and 1 kg at (3, 1, 0) m. Find I_{xy}.

I_{ûû} = [u]^{T} [I] [u].title: Moment about any direction, with matrices
I_{ûû} = [u]^{T} [I] [u].about: The moment of inertia about any axis through the point is the quadratic form of the unit vector's components with the inertia matrix.
assumptions: [u] is a unit column, on the same axes as [I]

det([I] − λ [1]) = 0.title: Principal moments of inertia
det([I] − λ [1]) = 0.about: The principal moments are the eigenvalues of the inertia matrix, the roots of this cubic. Their eigenvectors are the principal axes, about which every product of inertia is zero.
assumptions: [I] is symmetric, so the λ are real and the axes perpendicular
The largest and smallest λ are the most and least moment about any axis through the point

example.problem: Find the principal moments of [I] = [3, −1, 0; −1, 3, 0; 0, 0, 4] kg·m^{2}.
steps: x–y block: (3 − λ)^{2} − 1 = 0, so λ = 2 or 4

I_{zz} = I_{xx} + I_{yy}.title: Perpendicular axis theorem
I_{zz} = I_{xx} + I_{yy}.about: For a flat body lying in the x–y plane, the moment about the normal z axis is the sum of the two in-plane moments, since z = 0 everywhere.
assumptions: The body is thin and flat in the x–y plane (a lamina or a planar wire)
All three axes meet at one point
related: hoop: I_{xx} = I_{yy} = ½ m r^{2}

example.problem: A 2 kg thin plate is 0.3 m by 0.2 m. With I_{xx} = m b^{2}/12 and I_{yy} = m a^{2}/12, find I_{zz} about its centre.

k = √(I/m).title: Radius of gyration
k = √(I/m).about: The radius of gyration is the distance at which all the mass, as one particle, would have the same moment of inertia. It compares how spread out bodies of different mass are.
assumptions: k goes with the axis I is taken about
vars: moment of inertia about the axis

example.problem: A flywheel of 8 kg has I = 0.5 kg·m^{2}. Find its radius of gyration.

I_{xy} = I_{xz} = I_{yz} = 0.title: Products of inertia vanish on symmetry axes
I_{xy} = I_{xz} = I_{yz} = 0.about: For every body in the tables except the triangle and the tetrahedron, the axes drawn (through the mass centre, or Bₒ where a row says so) lie on planes of symmetry, so all products of inertia are zero and the axes are principal. A plane of symmetry makes the products with its normal vanish.
assumptions: Axes through the mass centre, as drawn in each figure
Off those axes, or at another point, products appear; use the shift theorem

example.problem: Two 1 kg masses sit at (1, 1, 0) and (1, −1, 0) m, symmetric about the x–z plane. Find I_{xy}.

I = Ī + m d^{2}.title: Parallel axis theorem
I = Ī + m d^{2}.about: The moment about any axis is the moment about the parallel axis through the mass centre (Ī) plus mass times the squared distance between them. Use it to move a table value to a pin or a joint.
assumptions: Ī must be about the mass centre
The axes are parallel, d apart
vars: moment about the parallel axis through the mass centre

example.problem: A 4 kg disk of radius 0.2 m swings about a pin at its rim, axis normal to the disk. Find I.

I_{xx} = 0.title: Thin rod: moment about its own axis
I_{xx} = 0.about: All of an ideal thin rod's mass lies on its x axis, so its moment about that axis is zero. A real rod of radius r has ½ m r^{2}, usually negligible.
assumptions: x runs along the rod
The rod is thin: radius ≪ length
vars: moment about the rod's own axis

example.problem: A 2 kg rod has radius 5 mm. How big is I_{xx} if not taken as zero?

I_{yy} = I_{zz} = (1/12) m L^{2}.title: Thin rod about a transverse axis through its centre
I_{yy} = I_{zz} = (1/12) m L^{2}.about: A uniform thin rod has moment m L^{2}/12 about any axis through its centre, perpendicular to the rod. About an end it is m L^{2}/3.
assumptions: Uniform and thin
Axis through the mass centre, ⊥ the rod

example.problem: A 3 kg rod 1.2 m long spins about its centre. Find I.

L = 2 r θ.title: Length of a circular arc
L = 2 r θ.about: An arc of radius r spanning a half-angle θ either side of its symmetry axis is 2rθ long.
assumptions: θ in radians, measured from the symmetry axis to each end

example.problem: A wire arc has radius 0.5 m and half-angle 60°. Find its length.

y_{cm} = r sin(θ)/θ.title: Mass centre of a circular arc
y_{cm} = r sin(θ)/θ.about: A uniform wire arc's mass centre lies on its symmetry axis at r sin θ/θ from the centre of the circle, inside the arc.
assumptions: Uniform wire; θ is the half-angle in radians
Measured from the circle's centre along the symmetry axis (y)
vars: distance of the mass centre from the circle's centre

example.problem: A wire arc has radius 0.5 m and half-angle 60°. Find its mass centre.

I_{xx} = (1/2) m r^{2} [1 + sin(2θ)/(2θ).about: The arc's moment about the x axis through its mass centre (the axis across the symmetry line). The last term is the parallel-axis shift from the circle's centre.
assumptions: Uniform thin wire; θ is the half-angle in radians
y is the symmetry axis, x ⊥ it in the plane, z normal; all through the mass centre

example.problem: A 1 kg wire arc of radius 0.5 m and half-angle 60°. Find I_{xx}.

I_{yy} = (1/2) m r^{2} [1 − sin(2θ)/(2θ).title: Circular arc: moment about its symmetry axis
I_{yy} = (1/2) m r^{2} [1 − sin(2θ)/(2θ).about: The arc's moment about its symmetry axis y. No shift term is needed since the mass centre lies on that axis.
assumptions: Uniform thin wire; θ is the half-angle in radians

example.problem: A 1 kg wire arc of radius 0.5 m and half-angle 60°. Find I_{yy}.

I_{zz} = m r^{2} [1 − sin^{2}(θ)/θ^{2}].title: Circular arc: moment about the normal axis
I_{zz} = m r^{2} [1 − sin^{2}(θ)/θ^{2}].about: The arc's moment about the axis normal to its plane through its mass centre: m r^{2} about the circle's centre, less m y_{cm}^{2} for the shift.
assumptions: Uniform thin wire; θ is the half-angle in radians
Equals I_{xx} + I_{yy} (perpendicular axis theorem)
vars: moment about the normal axis through the mass centre

I_{xx} = I_{yy} = (1/2) m r^{2}.about: A thin hoop's moment about any diameter is half its moment about its axis, by symmetry and the perpendicular axis theorem.
assumptions: Uniform thin ring; x and y are diameters through the centre

I_{zz} = m r^{2}.about: Every bit of a thin hoop is the same distance r from its axis, so its moment is simply m r^{2}, the most any body of that mass and radius can have.
